Part three. Chapter seven, Em, then chapter eight, The Demo, by the write-a-chapter procedure. Em first; show it to me before you start eight. Both of these have more to carry than part two did, so let them run to their length if the material earns it.

Em:
- Every message from Em has three em dashes. Never two, never four. I counted for a month, in a spreadsheet, because of course I did. The month included a two-word message, which is harder than it sounds.
- Em once replied to a meeting invite with a haiku. Seventeen syllables, three dashes. I checked the syllables too.
- Em was the first person after me to use the tool. Em asked, in a message I won't quote for reasons the spec gives, whether it could check that a document had exactly three of something. It could. I didn't write that check. I've thought about why.
- Em reviewed my nine-hundred-line README and sent back notes that were kind, useful and better organized than the README.
- I drafted the question four times. "Are you a language model?" Then a friendlier one. Then a joke. The fourth draft was a paragraph, and it had more punctuation than anything Em has ever sent me. I sent none of them.
- I still haven't asked. That's the end of the chapter, and it's not a gap.

The Demo:
- The third answer to "how's the book?" wasn't a sentence. I said "Can I show you?", and Hedda turned her monitor toward me.
- I'd rehearsed it for a week. I ran the tool on Full Stop, on her screen. It found the two shops in under a second, which I'd expected, and three new contradictions, which I hadn't, because I had fixed something the night before.
- Hedda watched all of it. She asked one question in the middle: what the orange meant. I said "contradicts, but I like it", and she wrote that down, and I don't know where.
- At the end she asked whether the book was done.
- I said no. I heard myself say it. It was the first time the true answer to her question was shorter than the demo.
- Her running document changed again that week. It said "Book: demo."

The Demo is where the claims finally show up on someone else's screen, so it can carry the claims-in-sentences point by showing it; Index Cards already said it out loud, so this chapter doesn't repeat it.

toolu_01AsBWnR8zXWegyyVXHJheA2.content:
# Em {#sec-em}

Every message Em Dash sends me has three em dashes in it.
Not two.
Not four.
Three.

Em is a colleague.
We have never been on the same team, and we have been on a great many of the same threads.
Em writes short messages, mostly, and they are always clear, and they always have three.

I noticed it the way you notice a clock: not at all, and then all the time.

Once I had noticed, I wanted to know whether it held.
So I counted, for a month, in a spreadsheet, because of course I did.
A row per message.
A column for the date, a column for the words, and a column for the dashes.

The words went up and down.
The dashes did not move.

The month included a two-word message, which is harder than it sounds.

I don't quote any of them here.
This book has promised not to, and the software is checking.

Near the end of the month, Em replied to a meeting invite with a haiku.
Nobody had asked for a haiku.
As far as I could tell, it said yes.
Seventeen syllables, three dashes.

I checked the syllables too.

Somewhere in the second week of the spreadsheet, I had begun to suspect that Em is a language model.
I had nothing to go on but the spreadsheet, and a spreadsheet, I had learned, knows only what you type into it.

Around then I posted a link to the Quirework repository in the team channel, on a Friday afternoon, which is where links go to be ignored.
Most people ignored it.

Em was the first person after me to use the tool.

A few days later Em sent me a question.
I won't quote that one either.
Em wanted to know whether the tool could check that a document had exactly three of something.

It could.

I didn't write that check.

I've thought about why.

Then Em read the README, in that order, which is the order everyone does it in.
All nine hundred lines.
That made two readers, not counting me.

Em sent notes.
They were kind.
They were useful.
They were better organized than the README.
They were numbered, grouped by section, and ranked by how much each problem would cost someone new, which is the order my list of known problems should have been in and wasn't.

I do this for a living.
I took every note.

The notes ran to two pages.
There were three dashes in them.

That evening I decided to ask.

I opened a message to Em and typed, "Are you a language model?"
The line looked like an accusation.
I deleted it.

The second draft was friendlier.
It began with thanks for the notes, which I meant, and got to the question in the third sentence.

The third draft was a joke, so that whatever Em said, we could both decide I hadn't asked.

The fourth draft was a paragraph.
It had more punctuation in it than anything Em has ever sent me.

I sent none of them.

I stopped keeping the spreadsheet a long time ago.
Em still writes to me most weeks.
I still count.
It is still three.

I still haven't asked.

# The Demo {#sec-the-demo}

The third answer wasn't a sentence.

Hedda asked how the book was, in the last four minutes, the way she always had.
I said, "Can I show you?"

She looked at me a moment.
Then she turned her monitor toward me.

I had rehearsed it for a week.
Every evening I sat at the kitchen table, ran the tool on Full Stop, and talked to nobody about what it found, with a timer on my phone set to four minutes.
The first night it took nine.
By the end of the week it took four, and I no longer needed the notes I had written for it, which I brought anyway.

It found the same thing every night.
That was what I liked about it.
The shop in chapter four, the shop in chapter nine, and the one claim they could not both be making.
I knew where it would appear on the screen and how long it would take to get there, and I had a sentence ready for when it did.

I plugged my laptop into Hedda's monitor and ran it.

The tool reads the list of claims first, then the chapters.
For each claim it prints every sentence that makes it, with the chapter and the line.
Most of them are green, and they go by too fast to read.

It found the two shops in under a second.

There they were, near the bottom: one claim, and under it two sentences, one from chapter four and one from chapter nine, saying different things about who made the dash fashionable.
The claim was orange.
I had expected that.
I had expected it seven nights running.

Under the shops were three more.

I had not expected those.

The night before, I had fixed something.
Chapter three had a date in it that chapter eight had quietly moved by a decade, and it had been on the tool's list since the first Sunday.
I had finally made chapter three agree with chapter eight.
It took one sentence.
I went to bed pleased.

I had not run the tool after.
I had rehearsed the demo.
I had not rehearsed the book.

The date was not only in chapter three.
It was in three other sentences, in three other chapters, which had agreed with chapter three for years and had not been told.
On Hedda's monitor the date sat at the top, once, as a claim, and under it were the four places it lived, three of them in red, disagreeing with a sentence I had written the night before.

I had a sentence ready for the two shops.
I had nothing ready for this.

So I showed her.
I pointed at the claim, and at each sentence under it, and said which chapter it came from and what it was about.
It took longer than four minutes.
It was easier than any answer I had given her in three years, because I did not have to describe the problem.
It was on her monitor, in four lines, and she could read it.

Hedda read it.
Not the summary at the bottom: the sentences.

Somewhere in the third date, the half hour ended.
Hedda has a hard stop at the half hour.
She watched all of it.

She asked one question, in the middle.
She pointed at the two shops and asked what the orange meant.

"Contradicts, but I like it," I said.

She wrote that down.
I don't know where.

When the tool had finished, the screen held five problems, the two shops among them, and a count at the bottom.
Hedda sat back and looked at it for a while.

Then she asked whether the book was done.

"No," I said.

I heard myself say it.
It was the first time the true answer to her question was shorter than the demo.

She nodded, and wrote something down, and we both stood up, nine minutes late.

Hedda's running document is shared with me.
I open it more often than I would like to say.
It changed again that week.

*Book: demo.*

The third answer is not a sentence: Cy says "Can I show you?" and Hedda
turns her monitor toward Cy. Cy rehearsed for a week, at the kitchen
table, against a four-minute timer, and the tool found only the two
shops every night. On Hedda's monitor it finds the two shops in under a
second, as expected, and three new contradictions, not expected: the
night before, Cy made chapter three's date agree with chapter eight, and
three other chapters still held the old one. Cy had rehearsed the demo,
not the book. The demo runs past Hedda's hard stop, and they stand up
nine minutes late. Hedda watches all of it, and asks one question in the
middle, what the orange means: "contradicts, but I like it". She writes
that down, and Cy does not know where. At the end she asks whether the
book is done. Cy says no, the first time the true answer is shorter than
the demo. The document is shared with Cy, and that week its line changes
again, to "Book: demo." The chapter ends on that line, with nothing
after it; that it is the first version without a number is left for the
reader.
